blocks.prompt: The Gorilla That Makes a New Bed Every Night
blocks.text: A gorilla is the biggest ape on Earth. A grown male can weigh more than two grown men. But a gorilla does not hunt. It eats leaves, stems, and fruit all day long. Gorillas live in families. One big male leads the family. His back turns silver as he gets older, so people call him a silverback. He keeps everyone safe. Every night each gorilla bends branches and leaves into a nest. It is a fresh bed, made in a few minutes. In the morning the family walks away and leaves it behind. That night, they build brand new ones.

blocks.prompt: The Biggest Ape in the Forest
blocks.text: A gorilla is the largest primate alive. A grown male can weigh over 400 pounds, and his arms are longer than his legs. He walks on his knuckles, resting his weight on the backs of his fingers. All that muscle is built on leaves. Gorillas are almost entirely plant eaters. A mountain gorilla can chew through 40 pounds of leaves, stems, and shoots in a single day. Leaves are not very filling, so gorillas eat for hours, then rest, then eat again. Gorillas live in families led by one older male. Around age twelve, the hair across his back turns silvery gray, which is why he is called a silverback. He decides where the family walks, where it eats, and where it sleeps. When he wants to warn a rival, he stands up, cups his hands, and beats his chest. Cupped hands make a hollow pok pok pok that carries more than half a mile through the trees. It looks like a fight. Most of the time, it is a way to avoid one.

blocks.prompt: Built of Leaves
blocks.text: Imagine an animal strong enough to snap a bamboo stalk in one hand, and then imagine it spending its whole life eating salad. That is a gorilla. Gorillas are the largest primates on Earth. A wild silverback can reach 400 pounds, yet nearly everything he eats is a leaf, a stem, a shoot, or a piece of fruit. He builds all that muscle out of plants, the same way an elephant does. Plants come with a catch. Leaves hold very little energy for their weight, so a gorilla has to process an enormous volume of them. A mountain gorilla may eat 40 pounds of vegetation a day, which takes hours of steady chewing. Then the family rests while all that green matter breaks down. A gorilla day is mostly eat, rest, eat, rest, move a little, repeat. Each family is led by a silverback, a male old enough that the hair over his back and hips has turned pale gray. He is not a bully. His job is to decide where the group goes, to break up squabbles between mothers, and to stand between his family and danger. Younger males, called blackbacks, wait their turn or leave to start families of their own. The famous chest beat belongs to him. He rises onto his legs, cups his hands, and drums, and the sound is not a slap but a hollow pok pok pok that travels more than half a mile through the forest. Researchers found that bigger males produce deeper beats. A rival hearing that sound learns the drummer's size without ever meeting him. The display is loud because it lets both animals skip the fight.

blocks.prompt: The Gentle Giant We Invented a Monster From
blocks.text: For most of the last two centuries, the gorilla was a monster. Western science did not formally describe the animal until 1847, and the mountain gorilla not until 1902. What arrived in Europe and America first were not observations but stories: an enormous black ape of the African forest, roaring, unpredictable, impossibly strong. Hollywood finished the job in 1933 with King Kong, and the picture set. A gorilla, everybody knew, was rage with arms. Almost none of it was true. Gorillas are the largest primates alive, and they are essentially vegetarian. A silverback of 400 pounds spends his day chewing leaves, stems, and shoots, then resting while the fiber breaks down, then chewing again. He has enormous canine teeth he almost never uses on anything but display. He lives in a family of females and young, and his role is closer to babysitter than warlord: he settles arguments, waits for slow infants, and puts his body between the group and any threat. Infants ride on his back. When western lowland gorillas find a patch of favorite food, they hum and sing to themselves while they eat. The chest beat, the gesture that built the monster, turns out to be an argument against violence. A silverback rises, cups his hands, and drums. The hollow pok pok pok carries more than half a mile through dense forest, and researchers have shown that larger males beat at lower frequencies. A rival can therefore measure his opponent from a distance, decide he cannot win, and leave. The display exists so the fight does not have to. Correcting the record took one stubborn person. Dian Fossey moved into the Virunga Mountains in 1967 and spent eighteen years living beside mountain gorillas, learning their voices, naming individuals, and publishing what they actually did all day. She also fought poachers, which is almost certainly why she was murdered in her cabin in 1985. Her work made mountain gorillas famous, and famous animals attract money. That money has done something rare. Mountain gorillas fell to roughly 250 animals in the 1980s. Today, guarded by rangers and funded largely by tourists who pay heavily to sit near them for an hour, there are more than a thousand. In 2018 the mountain gorilla was moved off the critically endangered list. It is one of conservation's few genuine wins, and it was paid for by the same species that invented the monster in the first place.

Chest-beat pitch signals body size (2021 study)
Downlisted from critically endangered in 2018

blocks.prompt: The Monster We Made, and the Animal That Was Always There
blocks.text: Two animals share the name gorilla. One of them is real. The invented one came first, at least for Europe and America. Western science did not formally describe a gorilla until 1847, when a missionary in West Africa sent home a skull; the mountain gorilla waited until 1902, when a German officer shot one in the Virunga range and the species was named after him. In the gap between rumor and evidence, imagination did the work. The gorilla arrived in the popular mind as a roar with fur on it, a forest demon of impossible strength and no restraint, and in 1933 King Kong nailed the portrait to the wall. The picture was so satisfying that it survived nearly a century of contradicting facts. The real animal is a large, slow, cautious vegetarian. Gorillas are the biggest primates alive; a wild silverback can pass 400 pounds. Nearly all of that is assembled from leaves, stems, shoots, pith, and fruit. Plant matter is poor fuel for its bulk, so a mountain gorilla may work through 40 pounds of vegetation a day, and the schedule that follows is not the schedule of a monster: eat, rest while the fiber ferments, eat, rest, move a short distance, eat again. Roughly half the daylight is spent doing nothing at all. Every evening, each gorilla old enough to be independent bends branches and leaves into a fresh nest, sleeps in it once, and abandons it at dawn. A creature that rebuilds its bed nightly and never reuses it is not organizing much of a rampage. Family life is quieter still. A group is one silverback, several females, and their young. He is called a silverback because at about twelve the hair across his back and hips fades to pale gray, and his authority is real but domestic: he chooses the day's route, breaks up squabbles, tolerates infants climbing on his head, and waits for the slow ones. Females carry a single infant for about eight and a half months, close to a human pregnancy, and nurse it for years. Western lowland gorillas hum and sing to themselves when the food is good, a habit researchers have recorded and catalogued. Individual gorillas can be told apart by the wrinkles above their nostrils, as unmistakable as fingerprints. Even the chest beat, the single gesture the monster was built from, argues the other way. A silverback stands, cups his hands, and strikes his chest, and the cupping matters: it makes a hollow pok pok pok rather than a slap, and the report travels over half a mile of thick forest. In 2021 researchers measured those beats and found that larger males drum at lower frequencies. The beat is therefore a broadcast of body size. A rival can hear it, run the numbers, and withdraw without either animal risking a wound. The display is not the prelude to violence. It is the substitute for it. Correcting the record cost a life. Dian Fossey settled in the Virungas in 1967 and spent eighteen years recording what mountain gorillas actually did, hour by hour, until she was murdered in her cabin in 1985, almost certainly by people whose poaching she had made unprofitable. Her data replaced the demon with an animal. The fame that followed turned out to be worth money, and the money turned out to be worth gorillas: rangers, patrols, and tourists paying heavily for one guarded hour on a mountainside. The population bottomed near 250 in the 1980s. It now exceeds a thousand, and in 2018 the mountain gorilla was downgraded from critically endangered to merely endangered, which in conservation counts as a triumph. So the ledger closes strangely. We imagined a monster, hunted the animal that inspired it, and then spent a fortune keeping that animal alive. The gorilla never changed. We did.
